inline.s: After walking for several days we reached Qujing Prefecture and came to Poshan, the very place where Zhuge Wuhou of old made his covenant of alliance with Meng Huo. There was an ancient temple here, and we put up for the night. I said to my companions: “This long journey of ours is not that of ordinary wandering monks. We must not simply go about admiring the scenery and neglecting true cultivation. We should buy a Luohan lamp here — a lamp above, with a reservoir of oil below — carrying it by day and using it for light by night. Each evening we take turns standing watch. After supper, at the hour of Xu, we light the lamp and sit gathered about it, each following the scripture he has studied, either reading the text or savoring its meaning, until midnight when we end the sitting. Let this be the established rule of our pilgrimage.” Everyone agreed to follow it.

We came to Pingyi Guard, passed out of the southern Yunnan border, and now touched the frontier of Guizhou. Going through Yizikong, we entered Puan Prefecture. After several more days we crossed Guansuo Ridge. This ridge is extremely lofty, a hundred li or more in circuit, and on its summit stands a military camp and a temple to Guansuo. A few days later we crossed the Pan River, where the mountain paths wind in curves, rising and falling steeply and dangerously. Within a moment a great rain poured down; the mountain streams and brooks became mountain torrents roaring like thunder, the winding paths all turned into watercourses, and a fierce wind blew in from all sides, forming whirlpools, so that one could hardly stand alone. The rain poured down from head and neck in great scoops, filling our clothes and trousers, cold to the very bone; we set our feet wide apart and moved as if riding a float-skin. When we loosened our belts to drain the water it gushed out like opening a sluice gate, and this happened several times. I said to the others: “The ancients who went seeking Dharma cast aside their very lives and did not think it hardship. Do not let this great rain make you retreat from your resolve to seek the Way; then in the future you will be able to boast to others how heroic our pilgrimage was!” Hearing this, everyone laughed, and we helped one another along, leaning on one another for support. Toward evening we reached the foot of the mountain and lodged at the Great Vow Temple. There we met a monk who had come from south of the Yangtze, and we asked him about the road ahead. He said: “These days pilgrimage is hardest of all. Everywhere there are gangs of the rivers and lakes, most of them doing the work of Mara. If they see a monk wearing a patchwork robe and sitting on a rush cushion they will not harm him; otherwise I fear your study and pilgrimage will meet with obstacles. I advise you, my friends, if you wish to have a peaceful and quiet journey, you had best exchange your baggage.” We rested ten days, then crossed the iron-chain bridge over the Pan River, where the cliffs are steep, the woods and bamboo thick and verdant, and the surging river dashes on like an arrow. This is indeed the vital passage linking Yunnan and Guizhou.

The next day we took the mountain path leading to Anzhuang Guard. The sand and stones were rough and uneven, the ridge winding and tortuous, and before long the soles of our shoes were worn through, flapping so that they could hardly be worn; we threw them away and walked barefoot. After several tens of li, we rested when night fell, and our feet were so swollen that the ankles were gone, hurting as if burned with fire and pierced with awls. In the middle of the night I thought: I have not a penny on me, and this is a solitary hermitage on a wild path where there is nowhere to beg. I should not linger here; I must set out at dawn. Then I thought again: worldly people, seeking fame and rank, wealth and honor, must still endure much hardship before they attain their wish. Today we have left home to cultivate and seek liberation from the cycle of birth and death — how can we retreat from the vow we first made just because we lack a pair of shoes! The next day I still gritted my teeth and pressed on. At first my heels hurt so much that I could not set them to the ground, and I crept along leaning on a staff; but after walking on five or six li, I could no longer feel that I had feet, and no longer felt the pain. There was no resting place along the way, and by evening I had covered more than fifty li, lodging for the night in a hermitage at Anzhuang Guard. The next day I begged a pair of straw sandals, and when I tried them on, my skin broke and blisters formed, but I paid no attention. A man of the rivers and lakes followed us for several days, and even when we rested for the night he did not leave. The next afternoon we came to a small stream crossed by a single log bridge over two zhang long. Chengzhuo and the others crossed first, and I walked slowly behind, the man trailing after me. Just as I reached the middle of the bridge, I suddenly let out a great shout, and he was so startled that he fell into the water. Pointing at him, I said: “From now on you should wash your heart and reform, and be a good man.” His face reddened to the ears, he climbed up the bank, hung his head, and took another road away.

Amid the manifold hardships we met on the road, none of my companions found them to be afflictions. Summer passed and autumn came, and in early October we at last reached Wugang Prefecture in Huguang, lodging at the Zhishui (Still Water) Hermitage. The abbot was named Yihui, a man of deep spiritual resolve; learning that we had come a long way from Yunnan, he kept us there for the winter. One day he invited me into his room for tea. I saw on the table a copy of the “Understanding of the Dharma Flower”, which I had once heard my teacher praise back in Yunnan, so it remained in my memory, and I wished to borrow it to copy, but I had no paper or brush. The abbot’s junior dharma-brother, whose Dharma name was Zhongli, was very studious, and seeing what I intended, he supplied everything I needed. That winter it snowed without cease every day, and the room was bare and open, the north wind whistling in. I wore only a single patchwork robe, and sat on the plank bed of the lodging monks with my head drawn in, copying the book; though my fingers were frozen stiff and chapped, and the ink and brush froze, I did not pause for a moment. The two dharma-brothers, seeing my firm resolve and diligence, grew all the more affectionate and respectful toward me, and gave me a padded jacket, which I received with shame — it was the first time in my life I had worn cotton clothing. Two or three of my companions took leave of us to go on pilgrimage to the sea. Chengzhuo and Juexin stayed with me.

This Wugang Prefecture lay within the fief of the princely clan of Min. There was a member of the Min clan named Yanli, fond of studying calligraphy and painting, who was acquainted with Master Yihui. In mid-October he came through the snow to the hermitage, bringing a large sheet of paper which he pasted on the wall, intending to paint a picture of “A lone fisherman in a straw cloak on a solitary boat, fishing the cold river snow”. He roughed it in with charcoal several times but still could not make up his mind. Standing by watching, I said: “In all painting, the idea must come before the brush; only when the brush is set down without further thought or hesitation can one convey its spirit. To deliberate back and forth like this, I fear, loses the natural wonder.” He turned his head to look at me and said: “Surely speaking is easy; doing it is really hard. Can you do it?” I smiled and said: “I know a little.” He handed me the brush and said: “Please paint!” I took the brush in hand, first composed the picture in my mind, then in one sweeping motion completed it, and set the brush on the table. He praised it deeply and said to Master Yihui: “Among those who have left home, there are by no means few hidden masters! Just hang this painting in the hermitage!” From then on he often came and sat with me in talk. He wrote out three scrolls in his own hand and gave them to me, Chengzhuo, and Juexin, recounting the story of his calling upon master painters everywhere.

On the fifth day of the first month, Master Heyi began to lecture on the Surangama Sutra at the Liang Family Hermitage, sixty li from the Zhishui Hermitage. Master Zhongli came to invite us along. Chengzhuo had never read the Surangama Sutra, and so set out first for the Wutai Hermitage in Baoqing Prefecture to pay a visit to Master Zhuan (
zhuān

) Yu; when the lectures were finished, he would come to the Liang Family Hermitage to join us. The three of us — myself, Master Zhongli, and Juexin — came to the Liang Family Hermitage. There were only a little over twenty in the audience, and each contributed one dan of rice and one tael of silver to form a fellowship (a joint share-out). Master Zhongli paid his contribution in full, but Juexin and I had only the patchwork robes on our backs and our rush cushions, with no money or rice to offer, and had meant merely to join in for the joy of it and leave. Master Zhongli then informed the lecturer of this, and the Master, knowing we came from the poor southern border of Yunnan, excused us from the rice and silver and graciously allowed us to attend the lectures with the assembly. I said to Juexin: “The Dharma is bestowed by the lecturer, but the food is provided by everyone’s contribution; we cannot receive it for nothing.” Thereupon the two of us volunteered for the miscellanies, washing the bowls and chopsticks, sweeping the floor and carrying water, without waiting to be called, doing whatever work there was. On the first day of the fourth month the lecture period came to a close. Zhongli stayed on, while Juexin and I took our leave and went to Baoqing Prefecture, lodging at the Great Requital of Kindness Temple.

I heard that in this temple there was a Master Ziru, a native of Yunnan, and went to pay respects to him, telling him the whole story of my leaving home and coming south. Master Ziru then addressed me as his junior dharma-brother. I asked him why he addressed me so, and he said: “I am a man of Jianchuan Prefecture, and left home to become a monk at Shishi Mountain. In my youth I studied the scriptures under the old Master Liangru, and relied upon that venerable elder for six years, deeply taking in his Buddhist teachings. To this day we have had no news of each other. Now that I see Master Shaoru, it is as if I see the venerable teacher himself. So if we speak of our Dharma lineage, I should call you my junior dharma-brother. In Yunnan, what scripture did you hear your teacher lecture on?” I answered: “I once heard the Dharma Flower and the Surangama, but only planted the seed of it; I did not grasp its meaning.” He asked again: “Where have you come from today?” I answered: “From the Liang Family Hermitage in Wugang Prefecture, and I only came here after hearing Master Heyi lecture on the Surangama.” Master Ziru said: “Master Heyi is my fellow cultivator and friend. You have arrived at just the right moment this time. Master Zhuan Yu has just brought out a new work, the Commentary on the Four Meanings of the Surangama, and the lay supporters who protect the Dharma have asked to have it printed and circulated. The Master has ordered me to expound it in this temple in his place; the audience already numbers over a hundred. There is just a vacancy for the post of managing the back hall — you may take on this office.” I said: “It is enough to give me a scattered place to lodge; the post of head of the seats I would not dare to accept.” Master Ziru said: “A lion’s cub has no need for such excessive modesty. I will provide you with monk’s robes and shoes and socks, and you may enter the hall and take up the duties.” I said: “I beg you to grant me two things: first, let me still enter the hall and sit and sleep with my patchwork robe and rush cushion; and second, I beg the abbot not to have someone offer me extra meals. If only I may hear the scriptures and taste the flavor of the Dharma, I shall be overflowing with gratitude and nothing more.” But Master Ziru disagreed and insisted that I change into new clothes. At the time there was a resident monk of the temple named Yexi, also among the audience, who had long followed Master Zhuan Yu.

The next day he went to the Wutai Hermitage to pay respects to the Master, and when the Master asked about the affairs of the lecture period, he reported my background and my entreaties to the Master. The Master said: “When I was young, at the Bamboo Grove Temple on the Northern Five Terraces, I relied upon Master Yuechuan and attended the lectures with the assembly; I too wore a patchwork robe and straw sandals, with a staff, a bamboo hat, and a rush cushion. Later I began to wander, to the Tiantai and the Southern Peak and other places, and onward to this Baoqing, and I was still the same, never changing. Because these lay patrons built this hermitage, and knelt on the ground holding clothes and shoes with both hands begging me to change, and would not rise if I refused, I followed their wish, also in order to give rise to their faith. I have often seen meditation monks unwilling to change this habit; they all love it, and it is rare to see one willing to walk a different path. Today to hear that this monk from Yunnan is not turned by circumstances — he truly resembles my own conduct in former days. Go back and tell Master Ziru to follow his original resolve and not to force him! In doing this one can instruct the assembly not to be greedy.” Master Ziru then granted me what I wished. Among the assembly there were some who praised my simplicity, and some who mocked me for seeking to be different; but to these praises and gibes alike I turned a deaf ear.

Three days after the lecture period began, the abbot ordered the four heads of the seats to lecture in turn, each to speak six times. The head of the western hall having gone out on business, and the prior pleading illness, only the chief of the hall, Master Kedu, remained — a dharma-heir of Master Wuxue of Jingci Peak on the Southern Peak, by nature simple, sincere, and fond of study, who shared my aspirations and with whom I felt a mutual respect. From the fourth fascicle of the Commentary on the Four Meanings of the Surangama onward, the two of us took turns expounding it to the very end. When the Dharma assembly came to a close, Master Ziru led the company to the Wutai Hermitage to thank Master Zhuan Yu. The Master happened to be seated cross-legged beneath an umbrella, whence his style “the Umbrella-Dwelling Daoist”. After Master Ziru had paid his respects, he returned to the Great Requital of Kindness Temple. The Master detained me, and gave me a meal beneath the umbrella; the one dish was a plate of bitter melon. The Master first took a bite with his chopsticks, and at the same time bade me eat. I put a piece in my mouth; it was bitter and hard to swallow, yet I dared not spit it out. Seeing this, the Master laughed and said to me: “First bitter, then sweet — so it is for one who cultivates the Way and becomes a good spiritual friend.” I bowed in thanks for his instruction. The Master said: “You have a little strength of bone. Where do you plan to go afterward?” I said: “When I set out from Yunnan, I was seeking Master Sanmei in order to receive the precepts, and after that to study as I pleased.” The Master said: “Master Sanmei is a true Vinaya master; you may go to him to receive the precepts. But as for ‘studying as you please’ — in the monasteries of the south, most lecture halls do not keep strict rules, and many people are arrogant and reckless. If you find it not to your liking, come back to me here; above all, do not drift along with the current and indulge yourself outside. In the future you will certainly be a pillar of the Dharma.” He then had his attendant bring a set of the works he had himself written and gave them to me, and once more enjoined and encouraged me, saying: “Learn my conduct and my practice.” I bowed, received them, and took my leave.

The next day I asked Chengzhuo to go with me on pilgrimage to the Southern Peak. Setting out from Baoqing Prefecture, we walked for five days, passed Yangliu Pool, climbed up over the back mountain, and roamed the Nine Dragon Flat and the Ancient Great Flat, on the side of which was a pool called the Pheasant Pool. When Master Sanmei came to this pool, a dragon had transformed into a pheasant and beat its wings up from the heart of the water, and Master Sanmei gave it the three refuges and five precepts. We also paid respects at Maoping and other temples, and rounding the Heavenly Pillar Peak and the Misty Cloud Peak, went down from the Zhurong Peak to the front of the Southern Peak Temple, where we lodged at the Tea-Bestowing Hermitage. There we met a wandering cloud-water monk and asked him about the road ahead. He said: “Now the bandits are raging, sweeping on through Changde, Tanzhou, Gongan, Jingzhou, and other places. The defenses everywhere are strict. The officers and soldiers are no better; they often seize the monks’ baggage and then falsely accuse them of being spies and arrest them, so that one has no place to lodge a grievance and suffers every misery. You masters must on no account go down the mountain!” Hearing this, Chengzhuo and I were not frightened in our hearts; I thought, could we have walked thousands of li on foot and come to naught! So we asked the abbot whether any other road led through. He said: “The world is in such chaos; it would be best to stay on here for a while and set out when all is peaceful. There is no need to be impatient!” I said: “My resolve is fixed, and time waits for no one! I beg you to point out another road, and I shall be very grateful.” He said: “There is indeed another road, but it is very desolate and few travel it, all of it mountains and deep ravines. You must go by way of Qianyang to Huitong, then to Lülin County, and past the Puan Cihua Temple; when you reach there, ask the way to Wanzai County, then to Ruizhou Prefecture, and you can reach the provincial city of Jiangxi. This road avoids the places where the wandering bandits are making havoc.” The next morning we set out along the route he had told us. Sure enough, ridge after ridge of mountains, no village in sight, utterly desolate; sometimes we went from morning meal straight on until evening, sometimes setting out without any breakfast at all. Every day we covered no less than seventy or eighty li. Only after half a month did we come round to the provincial city of Jiangxi, and lodged at the Tower Under the Pagoda Temple. After resting three days we went through Dean County, roamed Mount Lu, and paid respects at the Guizong, Kaixi, and Wuru temples.

One day we came to the Wansong (Ten Thousand Pines) Hermitage. As the sky was darkening we knocked on the door to ask lodging, but the monk of the hermitage glared at us in anger and shut the door with a slam, refusing us. By now it was quite dark, and the bright stars were shining. With no help for it, we had to find some place to stay the night. We saw a great rock jutting out over the side of the road, with a space of over a zhang underneath. We three squeezed in, set down our rush cushions, and sat waiting for dawn. After a while the gate of the temple opened again, and that monk came to drive us away once more. The three of us sighed that our conditions did not match, yet rather pitied the man for his folly; we paid him no heed, and sat on through the night by force of will. When the east was about to lighten, the three rose and went along the road. We came to Douyeping, ate a morning meal, and went on to roam the Drying Grain Stone and the Looking-Up-to-Sky Flat, and even wandered the Golden Bamboo Flat. As the sun was about to set in the west we came to the Donglin Temple and lodged there. The meditation hall of the temple was in the back. The cloud-water hall had only three rooms, utterly desolate: wild grass covering the ground a foot or more high, walls fallen and tiles gone, doors and windows without any covering. In the temple there was a Beamed Hall. We went in to pay respects to the Buddha, and found the dust thickly gathered and the filth of pigeons and sparrows everywhere. Chengzhuo and I swept the Buddha hall clean and set our rush cushions to the left of the Buddha image, planning to sit in Buddha-recitation through the whole night, that we might not have come in vain to this ancient White Lotus Society. But the monk in charge came out from within, reproached us for not first telling the officers before lodging privately in the great hall, and with a loud voice abused us and drove us out, all the way to the mountain gate. An old monk who lived there as a sponsor of the temple asked us to stay to eat, and let us lodge. Then the monk in charge came again to reproach the old monk, and even splashed water on the ground so that we could not sit or lie. Taking leave of the old monk, the three of us went out of the mountain gate.

I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: across many lives and births we must have planted karmic conditions displeasing to that monk in charge, and today we are receiving the retribution. Think of him as a good spiritual friend, helping us accomplish the practice of patience and forbearance; we must by no means give rise to a mind of resentment. But still we could find no place to lodge. Chengzhuo said: “When we were coming up just now, I saw a dense grove of trees on the road below; we can go there to pass the night.” We went down and sought the grove, but it proved to be an old grave. The three of us set down our rush cushions and sat on the ground. The open country stretched empty and still, without a sound; there was no moonlight, and it was pitch dark, so that we could not see our own fingers. When we had sat until the first watch of the night, we suddenly heard a cry: “Catch him!” and all around, voices shouting in unison: “Catch the thief!” I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “If he should chase us here in earnest, black and white confounded and no way to speak in our defense, then it will be our fixed karma.”

When dawn came, we heard in the distance the bells of post horses, and only then knew that the road outside was a highway; our hearts were a little at ease. The three of us came out of the grove and saw a man working in the fields. We went up and asked him why the shouting had risen in unison all around the night before. He said: “The wheat in the fields is ripe now, and we were guarding against thieves; that is why we all shouted together — merely to frighten off robbers.” At this the three of us burst out laughing.

We went at once to the Xilin Temple to pay respects, and passed the night there. The next day we reached Jiujiang Prefecture, when the sun had already sunk west. Every hermitage outside the city refused to take us in, saying the local authorities strictly forbade harboring outsiders, and told us to go across the river where there would be lodging. We had no choice but to cross the river on an empty stomach. When the boat reached midstream the ferryman demanded his fare, and I untied the cloth I used to bind my legs and gave it to him. Among those on the boat was a Daoist who, seeing the state we were in, paid our fare for us. After we landed, we asked someone nearby whether there was any place to lodge in the vicinity. He answered that there was no monastery close by, but if we went seventy li down the river embankment to Zaogang, there was a place called the Five Patriarchs’ Mother-Separation Mound, where there was a tea hermitage that received monks. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “We have been deceived. The tea hermitage ahead is still far, and the southwest wind is blowing hard; we had best hurry as fast as we can and not hesitate here.” The three of us braved the fierce wind, muffling mouth and face, and hurried along beneath the moon, reaching the place only in the small hours. We knocked on the door and begged lodging, and it was fortunate that the abbot, a man of compassion in spirit, rose at once and opened the door and bade us enter, asking why we were traveling so late at night. We told him all in detail. He gave a long sigh, felt the hardship of pilgrimage, and gladly prepared tea for us. I said in praise: if not for the hermitage at Jiujiang, how would this man’s depth of spirit be shown!

After breakfast the next day we asked him about the road ahead, and learned that the various patriarch-temples along the way had all fallen into ruin, and only by good fortune had the old Master Sanmei had them repaired (
qì

) and restored. We resolved to go and reverently visit them. We set out for Huangmei County, climbed Mount Poe, and paid respects at the sanctuary of the Fourth Patriarch; then on to Fengmao Mountain, the sanctuary of the Fifth Patriarch; up the High Mountain Temple to the sanctuary of Master Jingjian; over the Bell Ridge to the Old Temple, the sanctuary of the Thousand-Year-Old Caudex Master Baozhang; on to Qianshan County, the sanctuary of the Third Patriarch; and to Qingyang County, to worship at Mount Jiuhua. Looking down from the great hall we saw a hermitage and went to lodge for the night, but it provided no evening meal. The next morning we sat a long while waiting for breakfast, when we saw the abbot come to tell us: “The hermitage is poor and has no means; I can only give you an empty place, not provide meals. To eat you may go to the room-chiefs and beg a meal.” I said to my two companions: “The room-chief’s kitchen is a meat kitchen; where would there be pure food there? Let us go elsewhere!” Thereupon we went up to the hall and bowed before the Bodhisattva, and went down the mountain with empty stomachs. After walking more than ten li we came to a lodging hermitage and only then ate a little.

We arrived at Taiping Prefecture and heard that Master Rongwu was lecturing on the Dharma Flower Sutra at the Qingshan Temple, not far from the prefectural city. We gladly asked the way and went, reaching the temple just as the sun had set. Seeing that we all carried staffs, hats, and rush cushions, the monk in charge would not give us lodging. When we begged him again and again, he saw the day was far spent and hard to travel, and had someone lead us out of the mountain gate to a small local-earth-god shrine by the road to lodge. The three of us stacked our rush cushions and sat facing one another. I said: “Since we have come in quest of the Dharma, how can we return empty-handed!” Early the next morning we walked back to the temple, ate the morning gruel, sat through one session of the lecture, and then went down the mountain, begging food and asking the way of the villagers, and went on our way. At about the hour of Si on the tenth day, we reached Nanjing. From afar we saw the jeweled pagoda of the Bao'en Temple, its five colors soaring into the sky, gleaming in the sun. We went in, bowed, and circled the pagoda. By noon we were hungry with nothing to eat, and asked one of those who were circumambulating where there was a hall that received monks. Someone pointed to the Tripitaka Hall in the southern corridor and said: “There it is.” We went there, bowed to the Buddha, sat beside the steps of the hall, and saw monks coming and going, yet no one came forward to greet us. The three of us did not know the reason, so we rose and went out, where we met an old monk and asked him the cause. He said: “Nanjing is a place of lecture halls and meditation halls. If your clothes and shoes are neat and proper, you are a meditation guest, and someone receives you. You are wandering monks on pilgrimage, and so no one concerns themselves with you.”

We then entered the city and lodged at the Great Buddha Hermitage, west of the bell and drum tower. There was no great hall there, only a mat canopy of reeds spread over the Buddha image. The abbot was a man of genuine practice, receiving the assembly with a bowl of rice and delighted to see us. Knowing we came from Yunnan, he said: “The abbot of the Xingshan Temple here, whose Dharma name is Yinwu, is a landsman of yours. You may go there, and he will certainly take you in.” At noon the next day we reached there and were given lodging. We saw that the great assembly all ate rice from weevil-ridded, long-stored grain, and the vegetable was only ill-salted, stinking pickles of the meanest sort. When we went into the guest quarters to have a look about, we saw that the resident monks of the temple themselves ate fresh seasonal vegetables and clean white rice. The abbot’s disciple, named Kuoran, was also a man of Yunnan, and recognized our accent. That night he came to the cloud-water hall to claim kinship, and I said we were men of Guizhou. He asked again, seeming as though he wished to keep us. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “We have come over ten thousand li and should rely upon a good spiritual friend of virtue. Toward a man like this, who does not consider others, we would rather willingly accept hardship and privation than go near him.”

Hearing that Master Juewu was lecturing on the Surangama Sutra at the Yuanjue Hermitage, we went out of the city to listen. It happened that some good supporters were making a charitable offering of food to the monks. All monks from the ten directions who came sat on the floor of the Skanda Hall, with a dish of four kinds of vegetables for every two people. I happened to share a meal with a wandering monk. I myself was attentive to my deportment and ate slowly; but he never let his chopsticks pause, and in one breath finished off all four dishes. When the meal was done and we had gone out, I said to my two friends: “In the future, if we have the conditions to set out a meal for the assembly, let the vegetables be served in large bowls no matter how many kinds, and let everyone eat freely. In this way, on the one hand we can make everyone pay attention to a monk’s deportment, and on the other we can give rise to the assembly’s faith and reverence. A man like the one today has utterly lost the character of a monk — how is he different from a starving fellow!”

We went again to the Pude Temple to pay respects and wander about, and entered the meditation hall for lodging. That night we discussed the matter, saying: now the tenth month is nearly past, and it is too cold for traveling on the road. It would be better to stay here a while and set out again in the warm spring. After the gruel the next morning we asked the temple controller for a lodging-place, and he said: “I cannot give lodging even to two of you, let alone three.” Then he looked at me and said: “As for the lamp-attendant’s place in the bell-and-board hall, I can give it to you alone.” I said with a smile: “I am a clumsy fellow with rough hands and clumsy feet, and cannot trim the glazed lamps.” The three of us packed our things and went out of the mountain gate. I said to Chengzhuo and Juexin: “Since the monasteries of the capital will give none of the three of us lodging, let us for the time being scatter and pass the winter separately, and agree to meet on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. I hear that Baohua Mountain sets great store by studying the scriptures; I want to go there to study the Surangama Dharani.” Chengzhuo said: “Juexin and I will go to the Ancestral Hall; come over when you have finished studying the mantra.” I exchanged my rush cushion for a sleeping-mat with Juexin, and the three of us parted ways.

When I had climbed a little way up the slope of Baohua Mountain the sun had set, and I lodged at the Shimen (Stone Gate) Hermitage. At tea that evening I asked the abbot of the hermitage: “I hear Baohua set great store by the study of scriptures, and I wish to go.” The host said: “In the mountain there is an old head instructor, a man of Yunnan, who long dwelt in the northern capital. He has been on Baohua Mountain ten years and has read the great canon three times, and he delights most in those who study diligently. I too once studied scriptures under him. There are few people in the temple; there are four room-chiefs, and by good fortune everyone eats from a single pot, so no separate meals are made. Although all three meals are but thin gruel, the wandering cloud-water monks who come and go to worship the copper hall are all given lodging and food. Since you wish to stay on the mountain to study, you must set body and mind down and not mind the poverty and meagerness there.” The next morning I climbed the mountain, and reaching the resident temple, bowed to the Buddha, and then went about wandering here and there and paid respects to the resident monks for a whole day. In a subtle way I felt the place was familiar, as if I had been here before. I paid respects to the head instructor, bowed, and told him I wished to study the Surangama Dharani. The Master asked: “What place are you from? How many years have you been a monk? This mantra should be read through in advance until you know it well.” I said I was a man of Yunnan, had just left home to come south, and was illiterate, so I had not read it. Thereupon the Master consented, saying: “Since you have come to the mountain, you may work at the hall (washing bowls and delivering meals and the like), and lodge in the kitchen.”

When the eleventh month came, the weather was freezing. The washed bowls, stacked together, froze into a single mass and were hard to separate; so each time after washing them I dried them with a clean cloth, and the next morning when I used them they separated easily. For the water-drawer one man could not keep up the supply, and I helped carry water as well. The monk in charge of the kitchen, whose Dharma name was Liaoran, was young and quick. There were also room-chiefs (monks in charge of the storerooms) who each day measured out the rice and vegetables and handed them to the kitchen monk to cook into a meal or a soup. But once things passed through that kitchen monk’s hands, he would hold back a portion for himself. One day, when I came back from reciting the Surangama Dharani, he had kept back some rice and asked me to eat. I asked him: “The assembly eats gruel; where does this rice come from?” He said: “I keep it back for you out of good will, and you still question me!” I said: “A great man — how can he eat food of unknown origin!” And I rose and left. From then on the kitchen people banded together, shielding one another, and found it hard to let me live with them. That kitchen monk privately discussed with the controller that, since no one was in the board hall (the hall in the temple that kept the watch), I should be made to keep watch there, tending the incense and striking the board (in old times time was kept by the burning of incense, and at the appointed hour the board was struck as a signal). This hall was bare and open, with a wide monk’s bed; I slept there alone, as if in an ice cave. There was an old room-chief, a eunuch who had left home, who had the most compassionate heart of all, and pitying me for my high resolve in poverty, one dark night pushed open the door and came in, and whispered close to my ear: “Take this thing to ward off the cold!” Then he went out again.

I reached out to touch it; it seemed like wadding, but it was not soft, and when I covered myself with it it gave no warmth at all. When it grew light I looked at it, and it was an old padded quilt patched with countless patches. The thing was poor enough, but I was very grateful for the man’s kind heart. On the sixteenth day of the twelveth month I finished studying the mantra and went to thank the head instructor. The Master said: “On New Year’s Day of the coming spring, a layman Sang of the river-mouth town will come to the temple to perform the Emperor Liang Repentance; you should have the mantra read through and well-mastered by then. The fees from the repentance can pay for your own clothing and the like.” I had agreed with Chengzhuo and Juexin to meet on that day, so I had no heart for the matter. On the twentieth (
niàn

) day of the twelveth month, in the small hours before dawn, I got up and bowed three times toward the lodging of the head instructor, then turned back and went down the mountain. When I reached Dongyang I asked the way to the Ancestral Hall. After walking more than a hundred li, I arrived only as the sun sank west and the stars filled the sky, and asked whether Chengzhuo and Juexin were there. The monk in charge of the cloud-water hall said: “Several days ago the two of them went off together on pilgrimage to the South Sea. They left word that if Shaoru of Huashan came looking for them, he should follow on after.” Early the next morning I set out, and passing Niushou, met the sponsor Dunxiu, whom I knew from the Water Moon Hermitage in Guizhou; he insisted I stay for the new year. The next day, after eating a little, I left without saying farewell, and reached the Linggu Temple, on the very evening of the thirtieth of the twelfth month. The cloud-water hall had at its midst a good many of the rivers-and-lakes sort, noisy and distracting beyond measure, and no place empty to sit. I sat behind the panel of the door until dawn, ate some gruel, and set out.

Going out I met the abbot of the temple, whose Dharma name was Hongchuan, and he said to me: “Today is New Year’s Day; why must you go! Please come back and rest a few days.” Seeing his warm sincerity, I returned to the temple, took the midday meal, and then left Linggu Temple all the same. After walking twenty li I lodged in a small hermitage. On the second of the month I rested at the South Hermitage of Tugiao. On the third I unexpectedly met Chengzhuo on the road. I asked him: “The two of you went off together to the sea; how is it you have come back alone?” Chengzhuo said: “Juexin had already gone ahead to the sea when he reached Wuxi County. I arrived later at Hangzhou and heard that the old Master Sanmei was transmitting the royal precepts at the Old Path Ridge on Mount Wutai, so I turned back to look for you and go together.” I said: “The road to Mount Wutai is far, and whether the royal precepts are truly transmitted is not yet certain. It would be better to receive the precepts right here at the Gulin Hermitage in Nanjing. This Gulin Hermitage is the sanctuary founded by the Vinaya patriarch Master Gu (Master Guxin). What do you think?” Thereupon the two of us came to the Gulin Hermitage to receive the precepts. The guest-master (the monk in charge of receiving outsiders) said: “If you wish to receive the precepts, each of you must hand over one tael five mace of silver, and bring your own robe and bowl.”

Chengzhuo had clothes but no silver, and I had neither silver nor clothes. I had only a string of great amber prayer-beads of southern Yunnan in my bosom. I took it out and gave it to the guest-master, to be used toward a lodging-place and making robes. The guest-master took it in hand as if agreeing, turned, and went into the room. My eyes and ears were still keen, and I saw someone inside peeping out at us through the window, and heard a voice within say: “These two are rivers-and-lakes fellows; I fear the prayer-beads’ origin is not clear. On no account may you allow them lodging.” The guest-master came out of the room and said: “The resident establishment does not find it convenient to manage these affairs. Better that you prepare your robe and bowl and then come back.” I took back the prayer-beads and turned to go. He asked us to stay to eat, but I said: “A dragon must in the end return to the sea — how can it be trapped in an ox-trough!” I went at once out of the temple and found another hermitage to lodge in. The next day we crossed the Yangtze and reached Pukou.

On the fourteenth day of the first month we lodged at Red Heart Post-Station. Word spread that the wandering bandits were coming; men and women wept and cried aloud in a single wail, casting away their children and daughters, a misery beyond words. Chengzhuo and I had not a drop of water through our lips, and our bellies were quite empty; from dawn to dark we traveled in haste more than a hundred li, and lodged at the Third Post-Station. On the night of the fifteenth the wandering bandits broke through Fengyang city and burned the imperial tombs. Chengzhuo and I went north until we reached Xuzhou, and there at last rested our feet. The next day we crossed the Yellow River, but there was no boat, so we sat on the bank and waited until noon when we saw an official post rider’s horses; they had seized a boat and its boatman, and we took the crossing with them. Out in midstream the torrent was swift, and the boatman, in his cups, was weak-handed and strengthless; the boat was old and leaky. The official lost his head and called again and again on Heaven for protection, while we two gave ourselves wholly to Buddha-recitation. It happened that a light wind came up and blew the boat ashore in a reed thicket, and the two of us, seizing the reeds, waded to land and passed the night in a desolate hermitage.

The next day we began a long journey on foot, sometimes braving the wind and the rain, sometimes wearing the moon and the stars; now begging food in a village, now asking a meal of a plowman. Not until the first day of the third month did we reach the Great Wall pass; once through the Dragon Spring pass, we stepped onto the frontier of Shanxi, and at last came to the Old Path Ridge on Mount Wutai. The ten-direction hall of this temple, which receives traveling monks, stood outside the mountain gate. Chengzhuo and I settled in, and then went to the abbot’s quarters to pay respects to the old Master Sanmei. Two northern monks kept the gate, and said to us: “If you have incense-money, you may enter; if not, withdraw.” Seeing their rough and unyielding manner, we could see it was useless to reason with them, and went back to the ten-direction hall, sighing endlessly and saying: “We have climbed mountains and crossed rivers, not a few thousand li, to come and see a good spiritual friend face to face, and now because we have no incense-money we cannot be received — what is to be done?” Chengzhuo said: “There is no need to fret and be troubled. Wait until the gatekeepers go off to their gruel in the morning, and we shall go in ourselves to pay our respects.”
